ops.label: String functions
ops.detail: Taught Excel-equivalent first, then the SQL syntax.

ops.label: CONCAT — joins values into one string
No + operator for strings — every piece is its own argument, separators included
ops.detail: A space between first and last name is not a setting; it is a literal ' ' passed as an argument of its own. Same for a hyphen or a comma. Semicolon rule: it marks the end of a statement, so it is only required when running more than one query at once — optional for a single query.

ops.label: Takes as many arguments as you give it
ops.detail: Asked directly in class. Not capped at two — adding a separator already puts you at three.

ops.markdown:
```sql
SELECT *,
       CONCAT(customer_first_name, ' ', customer_last_name) AS full_name
FROM farmers_market.customer;
```

Three arguments, not two — first name, a literal space, last name.

**`SELECT *,` reads as "all the columns plus this extra one."** The star gives every original column of the table; the comma appends the computed one on the end. Nothing in the table is replaced or modified — the extra column exists in the output of this one query.

Table name is transcript-derived: the recording has both *customer* and *customers* and there is no notes PDF to settle it. Check the BigQuery panel before running this verbatim.

ops.label: Functions nest — the inner one resolves first
ops.detail: CONCAT never sees the column names. By the time it runs, its arguments are already values. An argument can be a literal, a column, or another function's result — anything that evaluates to a value. This is the mechanism the manual proper-case build depends on.

ops.title: CONCAT — the same query, one step apart

ops.markdown:
---

Add nesting and the shape does not change — only the arguments do:

```sql
SELECT *,
       CONCAT(UPPER(customer_first_name), ' ', LOWER(customer_last_name)) AS new_name
FROM farmers_market.customer;
```

Read it inside-out, which is the order it runs: `UPPER(...)` produces a value, `LOWER(...)` produces a value, and CONCAT receives three things — a value, a literal space, a value — and glues them.

ops.label: SUBSTR(value, start, length) — a piece of a string
1-indexed — SQL has no zero index
ops.detail: Asked explicitly in class and answered emphatically; repeated again at the end of the session. The first character is position 1. The one to actively unlearn if you have written Python.

ops.label: The third argument is a length, not a stop position
ops.detail: The instructor calls it the "stop" throughout. It is not one. The two coincide only when the start is 1, which is the case in his first examples, so the slip goes unnoticed. His own later example settles it: SUBSTR('Shankar', 2, 6) returns six characters starting at position 2 — a stop position would return five.

ops.label: Omit the length and it runs to the end of the string
ops.detail: The fix for hard-coding. SUBSTR(name, 2) gives everything from the second character onward whatever the name's length — writing 6 works for Shankar and breaks for Anu. Leave the length off and the query stops caring how long the input is.

ops.markdown:
Goal: `shankar` → `Shankar`, without a built-in.

```sql
SELECT CONCAT(
         UPPER(SUBSTR('shankar', 1, 1)),   -- first character, capitalised
         LOWER(SUBSTR('shankar', 2))       -- everything from the 2nd character, lowercased
       );
```

Two halves, each three levels deep — the nesting rule is what makes it readable. **Left half:** take one character starting at position 1, upper-case it. **Right half:** take everything from position 2 onward — no length argument, so the name's length does not matter — and lower-case it. CONCAT joins them.

**This CONCAT takes no space argument.** It is two halves of one word, not two words. The space in the full_name query was there because a first and last name are separate words; nothing about CONCAT requires one.

cells.c-expr: A negative start does not reverse the reading direction
cells.c-result: You start further back and still move forward, left to right — which is why -3 gives kar, not rak

cells.c-expr: The pattern that falls out: last n characters
cells.c-result: Start at -n and give no length

ops.label: INITCAP — proper case in one call
ops.detail: SELECT INITCAP('shankar') returns Shankar. Everything the manual build assembles collapses into a single call.

ops.label: BigQuery only — does not exist in MySQL
ops.detail: Asked directly, answered directly. This is why the manual CONCAT/UPPER/SUBSTR build was taught first — it is the MySQL route, not a warm-up to discard once the shortcut appears. First time the intro class's 90/10 rule bites in practice: most syntax carries across vendors, and the slice that does not fails outright rather than degrading. The instructor undertook to call out anything else in the module that will not carry over.

ops.label: Look functions up in the docs rather than memorising them
ops.detail: Pointed at the BigQuery SQL documentation. The right instinct because the function list is vendor-specific: what you hold in your head is what you want to do, the docs say whether this vendor names it, and the manual build covers you when it does not.

ops.markdown:
Filtering is **a subset of the rows you already have** — not a different table, not a transformed one. Same rows, fewer of them.

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE product_id = 'P1';
```

**Rule 1 — WHERE is written after FROM.** Until the engine has the table, it has nothing to filter.

**Rule 2 — the column you filter on must exist in the table.** WHERE has one condition in order to work: the column must be present in what FROM brought back. The instructor's prediction — most of the errors you will make in advanced functions come from forgetting this one line.

**Data grain.** Each row of the whiteboard table is one *order*, not one customer, which is why the same customer and product can repeat with a different sales figure. There is simply no order ID column shown.

ops.title: What WHERE can and cannot see

ops.markdown:
Create a column in SELECT and you **cannot** filter on it:

```sql
SELECT quantity * cost AS revenue FROM ...
WHERE revenue = 100          -- fails: no such column
```

But you **can** write the expression out:

```sql
WHERE quantity * cost = 100  -- works: both are real columns
```

The arithmetic is not the problem — WHERE will happily compute. What it will not do is resolve a name that SELECT invented.

The asymmetry looks arbitrary at this point in the lecture. It stops being arbitrary at the order of execution, which exists to explain exactly this.

cells.c-want: All four cells are about ONE column
cells.c-eg: one value or several — keep or exclude

ops.title: Why OR, not AND, on one column

ops.markdown:
Written the long way, "P1 or P2" is:

```sql
WHERE product_id = 'P1' OR product_id = 'P2'
```

**AND would be wrong, and the reason is the point, not the rule.** AND requires both conditions true **of the same row**. No single row has a product that is simultaneously P1 and P2 — there is no such product. Ask for it with AND and you get zero rows back, every time.

This is the mistake that feels most natural, because *"show me products P1 and P2"* is how you would say it out loud. The English word is exactly the wrong operator.

**IN is that OR chain with the repetition removed.** At five or six values, repeating `column = value OR column = value` stops being convenient. IN is not a different kind of operator that happens to take a list — its inherent meaning **is** OR.

**Quoting.** Text and dates are wrapped in quotes; numbers are not — give the number directly.

**Quoted text is case-sensitive.** It is stored as text and you are asking for an exact match, so `'edwards'` does not find `Edwards`. Nothing warns you — the row is simply absent.

**`!=` and `<>` are the same operator.** Two spellings of "not equal to"; use whichever you prefer. Confirmed twice in class.

**Semicolons.** A semicolon marks the end of a *statement*, so it is only required when running more than one query at once. Running a single query, it is optional — which is why omitting it produces no error rather than the failure a newcomer expects.

ops.markdown:
```sql
SELECT *,
       ROUND(cost_to_customer_per_qty * quantity, 2) AS amount
FROM farmers_market.customer_purchases
WHERE customer_id = 4
ORDER BY market_date;               -- 71 rows
```

**This is the two-rules note in the wild.** `amount` is invented in SELECT; the filter is on `customer_id`, a real column. Had the task been "everything over 100", the multiplication would have had to be written out in WHERE.

**The "1 of 50" trap.** Half the class reported 50 rows. That is BigQuery's page size, not the result size — page two carries the remaining 21. A silent wrong answer, not an error.

**Type `FROM` before `SELECT`.** Once BigQuery knows the table it autocompletes the column names. You write in execution order and let the tool help.

**`ORDER BY market_date` sorts the result by that column, ascending by default** — it is used here but never taught in this lecture. Take it as sorting only; the mechanics come later.

`cost_to_customer_per_qty` is transcript-derived and low-confidence — only "cost to customer" was spoken, and no notes PDF exists to settle it. Check the panel before running this verbatim.

ops.title: Operator precedence — not taught in class

ops.markdown:
```sql
WHERE product_id > 3 AND product_id < 8 OR product_id = 10;   -- 5 rows: 4,5,6,7,10
```

This returns the right answer **only because AND binds tighter than OR** — the engine reads it as `(product_id > 3 AND product_id < 8) OR product_id = 10`.

**The lecture never raises precedence.** This caution comes from the extraction, not the instructor. Worse, he said elsewhere that brackets "have no impact" — true in the `BETWEEN` context where he said it, not a general rule.

Change the intended grouping and the query silently returns a different set. **Parenthesise mixed AND/OR conditions, always.**
**`>` is not inclusive.** `WHERE product_id > 3` excludes product 3. Use `>=` when you want the boundary.

ops.title: BETWEEN — inclusive, and still an AND

ops.markdown:
```sql
WHERE product_id BETWEEN 4 AND 7    -- returns 4, 5, 6 and 7
```

**Inclusive of both bounds.** The analogy given: if you work between 2 and 4, both 2 and 4 are your working hours. Contrast `>`, which excludes its boundary — that inconsistency is why it is worth stating.

**You write the column name once**, rather than twice as with `> ... AND < ...`.

**The off-by-one when rewriting.** `product_id > 3 AND product_id < 8` becomes `BETWEEN 4 AND 7`. Same five rows, different literals, because one form is exclusive and the other inclusive.

It is still an AND underneath. One value satisfying both bounds at once is exactly what makes a range an AND — BETWEEN is shorthand, not a third operator.

Task: the vendor booth assignment for vendor 7 for all dates between 3 April and 16 May 2019, both dates included.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM farmers_market.vendor_booth_assignments
WHERE vendor_id = 7
  AND market_date BETWEEN '2019-04-03' AND '2019-05-16';   -- 13 rows
```

Two conditions on two different columns joined with AND — and here the range is itself one of the two conditions.

**The SQL date format is `YYYY-MM-DD`** — largest unit first, so it cannot be read as a different date.

`vendor_booth_assignments` is the **lowest-confidence identifier in the source**: the transcript has "BVA table" and "vendor booth assignment", and Scaler's own auto-notes call it `vba`. Verify it in the BigQuery panel before running this.

**Date literals take `YYYY-MM-DD`, with no spaces inside the quotes.** Several students hit this live. A date literal is a *string* the engine parses into a date; a space is not in that grammar, so the parse fails before any comparison happens. This failure is loud — unlike the case-sensitivity one above, which returns a plausible wrong answer.

**There is no `IN BETWEEN`.** `BETWEEN` takes a range; `IN` takes a bracketed list. They do not combine.

**Where the brackets claim is true.** He said it about a `BETWEEN` clause with no mixed AND/OR — and there it holds: brackets change nothing and are purely for readability. The claim is sound in its own context and wrong as a general rule, which is the whole of the problem with it.

ops.value: A range on one column (or its BETWEEN shorthand)

ops.title: IN with mixed case — the silent 3 rows

ops.markdown:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM farmers_market.customer
WHERE customer_last_name IN ('Diaz','Edwards','Wilson');   -- 4 rows
```

Three values, one column, keep them. Four rows rather than three, because two customers share a surname.

**Then he wrote `'edwards'` in lower case, and the result dropped to 3 rows.**

Nothing errored. No warning appeared. The query ran, returned a well-formed result, and one row was simply gone. Without being told to expect 4, you would have shipped 3. This is the expensive bug — a malformed date literal stops you, this one does not.

**The fix — normalise both sides:**

```sql
WHERE LOWER(customer_last_name) IN ('diaz','edwards','wilson')   -- 4 rows
```

`LOWER()` runs against the column value first and *that* is what gets compared against the list. Both halves have to change — lower-casing the column while leaving `'Edwards'` capitalised in the list fixes nothing.

ops.title: WHERE and SELECT — what each can see

ops.markdown:
---

**And the same boundary from the other side.** Applying `LOWER()` in WHERE does not lower-case the output — the displayed values come back exactly as stored, capital E and all. Only a function applied in **SELECT** changes what you see.

WHERE computes freely — arithmetic, `LOWER()`, whatever you like — but everything it computes is scratch work, discarded once the row has passed or failed. Nothing it does reaches the output.

- **WHERE decides which rows come back.**
- **SELECT decides how they look.**

The two clauses share results in neither direction.

**Quoting.** Text and dates are wrapped in quotes; numbers are not — give the number directly.

**Quoted text is case-sensitive.** It is stored as text and you are asking for an exact match, so `'edwards'` does not find `Edwards`. Nothing warns you — the row is simply absent. The fix is to normalise both sides: `LOWER(column) IN ('lower','case','list')`.

**`!=` and `<>` are the same operator.** Two spellings of "not equal to"; use whichever you prefer. Confirmed twice in class.

**Semicolons.** A semicolon marks the end of a *statement*, so it is only required when running more than one query at once. Running a single query, it is optional — which is why omitting it produces no error rather than the failure a newcomer expects.

**`>` is not inclusive.** `WHERE product_id > 3` excludes product 3. Use `>=` when you want the boundary.

**Date literals take `YYYY-MM-DD`, with no spaces inside the quotes.** Several students hit this live. A date literal is a *string* the engine parses into a date; a space is not in that grammar, so the parse fails before any comparison happens. This failure is loud — unlike the case-sensitivity one above, which returns a plausible wrong answer.

**There is no `IN BETWEEN`.** `BETWEEN` takes a range; `IN` takes a bracketed list. They do not combine.

ops.label: FROM
ops.detail: Go to the kitchen. You cannot do anything until you are there — which is why WHERE is written after FROM.

ops.label: WHERE
ops.detail: Keep only the red spoons. Filtering happens before sorting: sorting every spoon of every colour and then discarding most of them is work done on rows that were never going to survive.

ops.label: SELECT
ops.detail: Now you are holding the spoons. This is the move that explains everything: a column aliased here does not exist when WHERE runs, and a function applied in WHERE has already finished by the time this decides what to display.

ops.label: ORDER BY
ops.detail: Arrange them by length, longest first.

ops.label: OFFSET
ops.detail: Skip the longest one. You write LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1, but the engine skips first — "the second and third longest" is only meaningful in that order.

ops.title: The order you write vs the order it runs

ops.markdown:
**Written:**

```
SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT → OFFSET
```

**Executed:**

```
FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → OFFSET → LIMIT
```

Two differences. **SELECT falls from first to third.** **LIMIT and OFFSET swap.**

The task the analogy came from: *go to the kitchen and get me the two red spoons that are second and third longest.*

The step the instructor pressed hardest on is filter-before-sort. Keeping only the red spoons before arranging them by length is not a preference — sorting every spoon of every colour and then throwing most of them away is work done on rows that were never going to survive.

---

**And here is why, in one line: SELECT executes after WHERE.**

A column aliased in SELECT does not exist yet when WHERE runs, so there is nothing to resolve — WHERE is not refusing to look the name up, the name has not been created. And `LOWER()` in WHERE cannot change the output because WHERE has already finished by the time SELECT decides what to display.

Both halves of the boundary are the same fact: **WHERE runs, then SELECT runs, and nothing passes backwards.** The rule is not a restriction the language imposes — it falls out of the order, which means it can be derived rather than remembered.

Four quizzes ran. The player exposes their timestamps but not their text, so the questions are reconstructed from the spoken walkthrough.

**Joining with a separator.** Producing `Jan-2020` from a month and a year. The misconception being tested is the `+` operator, which SQL does not have for strings — the hyphen is passed to CONCAT as its own argument, exactly like a space. See the CONCAT branch.

**The last two characters of a name.** The safe form is the one on the negative-start table: start at `-n`, give no length — `SUBSTR(name, -2)`.

⚠️ **The demonstration in class does not match its own question.** He worked through `SUBSTR(name, -4, 2)` against Jesse, Brian and Walker — that takes two characters starting four from the end, which for *Walker* is `ke`, not `er`. Without the option text there is no way to tell whether that was the correct answer or a distractor being ruled out. Do not try to reconcile it; use the safe form.

**All information about a named customer.** Two things: `==` does not exist in SQL — comparison is a single `=`, and several students picked an option using the Python spelling. And the correct option handled the **case** of the name, which is the mixed-case failure from the IN section. "All info" is the cue for `SELECT *`.

**One customer, excluding one date.** Answered with AND, because these are two different columns — the name must equal A and the date must not equal 2019-02-04, both true of the same row. Straight application of the can-one-row-satisfy-both test.

Option letters are deliberately not recorded. Two of the four are contradicted in the recording, and a letter with no option text points at nothing even when it is right.

Two distinct causes, both diagnosed live in class.

**1. The table name is being typed wrong.** The reliable check: click the table in the BigQuery panel → three dots → **Query** → run `SELECT *`. Whatever name BigQuery fills in for you is the name to use.

This is the procedure that settles every identifier on this board without guessing — `customer` vs `customers`, `vendor_booth_assignments` vs `vba`, the real spelling of `cost_to_customer_per_qty`. The source for this lecture is a machine transcript with no notes PDF behind it, so the panel is the only authority.

**2. The table was never uploaded, or uploaded incompletely.** All 10 `farmers_market` tables must be uploaded, not just the one you need. Re-uploading with auto-detect fixes tables that appear in the panel but return nothing.

ops.title: NULLs — deferred, and a known hole

ops.markdown:
Asked in class. The module **will** cover what NULL is, how to treat it and how to replace it — and **none of it was taught in this lecture**.

Worth registering rather than leaving implicit: every filter on this board assumes the column has a value. What `WHERE product_id != 1` returns for a row whose `product_id` is NULL was never addressed, and it is not something to guess at from the rules given here.
